activities.title: Retry Budgets, Exponential Backoff, and Jitter

source_resources.title: Exponential Backoff And Jitter
source_resources.author: Marc Brooker, AWS Architecture Blog
source_resources.license: Amazon Web Services site content / linked reference
source_resources.permission_basis: Lawful external technical reference under public blog terms.
source_resources.prerequisites: Retries, timeouts, and basic probability of correlated load.
source_resources.selection_rationale: Detailed practitioner reference proving that full jitter (sleep = random_between(0, min(cap, base*2**attempt))) prevents synchronized retry storms and reduces total work during contention.
source_resources.known_availability_limitations: Public AWS blog post; stable URL since 2015.
source_resources.safe_fallback: The backoff exercise is implemented in pure Python with a local flaky stub; the derivation of jitter benefits is fully reproduced in lesson instructions.

compared_candidates.comparison_rationale: Product-scoped truncated exponential backoff recipe; Brooker's analysis explains why jitter matters, not just what to configure.
Library implementation reference; the AWS article supplies the comparative evidence (with/without jitter) that anchors the lesson.

source_resources.relevant_timestamp: Adding Backoff; Adding Jitter (Full Jitter, Equal Jitter, Decorrelated Jitter)

source_resources.title: Site Reliability Engineering, Chapter 22: Addressing Cascading Failures
source_resources.author: Mike Ulrich, in Site Reliability Engineering (eds. Betsy Beyer, Chris Jones, Jennifer Petoff, Niall Richard Murphy; Google)
source_resources.permission_basis: Lawful external hyperlink to Google's free web edition, published under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (Copyright 2017 Google, Inc.; published by O'Reilly Media); no text is imported.
source_resources.selection_rationale: Primary analysis of how unbounded retries amplify partial outages into cascading failures, motivating hard retry budgets and deadlines in agent runtimes.
source_resources.known_availability_limitations: Free online HTML edition hosted by Google; pagination differs from print.
source_resources.safe_fallback: The retry-amplification scenario and budget arithmetic are fully reproduced in the lesson's worked example.

compared_candidates.comparison_rationale: Broader stability-pattern catalog (circuit breakers, bulkheads); the SRE chapter is free and directly quantifies retry amplification.

compared_candidates.candidate_name: AWS Builder's Library: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter
compared_candidates.comparison_rationale: Strong companion article; the SRE chapter frames the failure mode (cascading overload) that the retry budget defends against.

source_resources.title: Python Standard Library: subprocess - Subprocess Management
source_resources.author: Python Software Foundation
source_resources.permission_basis: Lawful external reference under PSF open documentation terms; no source text imported into curriculum content.
source_resources.prerequisites: Processes, arguments, exit codes, and context managers.
source_resources.selection_rationale: Normative reference for subprocess.run(timeout=...), TimeoutExpired, DEVNULL stdin, and the documented kill scope: timeout terminates the child process; it does not define process-tree cleanup semantics.
source_resources.known_availability_limitations: Hosted on python.org; versioned per CPython release.
source_resources.safe_fallback: The kill-boundary experiment runs entirely in the standard library, so the documented semantics are exercised offline.

compared_candidates.candidate_name: POSIX standard: process creation and termination
compared_candidates.comparison_rationale: Formal POSIX semantics; the Python docs map directly onto the commands learners type.
Third-party tree enumeration; the exercise deliberately demonstrates the stdlib boundary before reaching for helpers.

source_resources.relevant_timestamp: Using the subprocess Module (subprocess.run timeout) and Notes: Timeout Behavior

source_resources.title: Linux man-pages: credentials(7) and setpgid(2) - Process Groups and Sessions
source_resources.author: Linux man-pages project (Michael Kerrisk et al.)
source_resources.permission_basis: Lawful external technical reference under open man-pages terms.
source_resources.prerequisites: POSIX processes, signals, and fork/exec model.
source_resources.selection_rationale: Normative reference for process-group semantics (PGID, sessions, killpg): the mechanism a runner must use to signal a whole descendant tree, which the lab runner and subprocess timeout path do not employ.
source_resources.known_availability_limitations: Hosted on man7.org; mirrors exist on every Linux system via man credentials.
source_resources.safe_fallback: Process-group behavior is demonstrated live with os.setsid and process inspection; local man pages cover the same text offline.

compared_candidates.comparison_rationale: Formal standard text; the man page presents the same contract with implementation notes learners can test directly.

compared_candidates.candidate_name: Advanced Programming in the UNIX Environment (Stevens), Chapter 9
compared_candidates.comparison_rationale: Detailed textbook treatment of sessions and job control; the man page is the free, always-current operational reference.

source_resources.relevant_timestamp: credentials(7) DESCRIPTION: Process group and session

source_resources.title: Linux man-pages: namespaces(7) - Overview of Linux Namespaces
source_resources.author: Linux man-pages project (Michael Kerrisk et al.)
source_resources.permission_basis: Lawful external technical reference under open man-pages terms.
source_resources.prerequisites: Processes, mounts, network interfaces, and cgroups basics.
source_resources.selection_rationale: Normative reference enumerating the eight Linux namespace types; establishes what genuine OS-level isolation requires (mount, PID, network, user namespaces plus seccomp and cgroup limits), all of which the learning project deliberately does not provide.
source_resources.known_availability_limitations: Hosted on man7.org; identical content ships with every Linux distribution.
source_resources.safe_fallback: Namespace concepts are analyzed against project code, not exercised; unshare(1) examples are optional enrichment.

compared_candidates.comparison_rationale: Product view assembling namespaces and cgroups into containers; namespaces(7) supplies the primitive inventory the lesson enumerates.
Strong narrative walkthrough; the man page is the maintained reference surface.

source_resources.title: Firecracker: Lightweight Virtualization for Serverless Applications
source_resources.author: Alexandru Agache, Marc Brooker, Alexandra Iordache, Anthony Liguori, Rolf Neugebauer, Phil Piwonka, Diana-Maria Popa
source_resources.permission_basis: Lawful academic reference under USENIX open-access terms.
source_resources.prerequisites: Virtualization basics, KVM, process isolation, and threat models.
source_resources.selection_rationale: Primary literature on production multi-tenant code execution: Firecracker wraps workloads in hardware-virtualized microVMs because containers alone are not a sufficient security boundary, the reference standard for what genuine isolation means.
source_resources.known_availability_limitations: Freely available via USENIX; PDF and slides hosted on usenix.org.
source_resources.safe_fallback: The isolation-layer analysis compares documented properties only; no virtualization is launched in the lesson.

compared_candidates.comparison_rationale: User-space kernel interception alternative; Firecracker's hardware boundary provides the stronger reference point for the guarantee matrix.
VM-backed container runtime; Firecracker's NSDI paper supplies the peer-reviewed threat-model justification.

source_resources.title: Python Standard Library: ast - Abstract Syntax Trees
source_resources.author: Python Software Foundation
source_resources.permission_basis: Lawful external reference under PSF open documentation terms; no source text imported into curriculum content.
source_resources.prerequisites: Python syntax, parse trees, and compile pipeline basics.
source_resources.selection_rationale: Normative reference for ast.parse used by scripts/check_snippets.py as the static admission gate: AST rules inspect source structure before any execution and cannot evaluate runtime behavior.
source_resources.known_availability_limitations: Hosted on python.org; grammar evolves between minor versions.
source_resources.safe_fallback: Every AST check in the lesson runs in the standard library; no external validator is fetched.

compared_candidates.comparison_rationale: Production AST linter; the stdlib ast module is the minimal sufficient tool for the admission-gate exercise.
Security-oriented AST rules; deliberately cited as a comparison to show AST gating is necessary but never sufficient for safety.

source_resources.title: Kubernetes Documentation: Resource Management for Pods and Containers
source_resources.author: Kubernetes Documentation Contributors
source_resources.permission_basis: Lawful external technical reference under Creative Commons license.
source_resources.prerequisites: Containers, CPU/memory accounting, and QoS classes.
source_resources.selection_rationale: Primary reference for cgroup-enforced resource limits (CPU throttling, memory OOM-kill): demonstrates that production limits are kernel-enforced accounting, contrasted with the project's application-level counters.
source_resources.known_availability_limitations: Public documentation; behavior details depend on cgroup v1 vs v2 deployments.
source_resources.safe_fallback: The lesson contrasts documented cgroup semantics with the project's counters; no cluster is required.

compared_candidates.comparison_rationale: Kernel-level primitive reference; Kubernetes docs present the enforcement outcome (throttle vs OOM-kill) learners recognize from operations.
Single-host flag surface; Kubernetes documentation covers limit semantics plus QoS classification.

source_resources.relevant_timestamp: How Kubernetes applies resource requests and limits
